# Amphiphilic shuttle peptide delivers base editor ribonucleoprotein to correct the CFTR R553X mutation in well-differentiated airway epithelial cells

## Abstract

Base editing could correct nonsense mutations that cause cystic fibrosis (CF), but clinical development is limited by the lack of delivery methods that efficiently breach the barriers presented by airway epithelia. Here, we present a novel amphiphilic shuttle peptide based on the previously reported S10 peptide that substantially improved base editor ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery. Studies of the S10 secondary structure revealed that the alpha-helix formed by the endosomal leakage domain (ELD), but not the cell penetrating peptide (CPP), was functionally important for delivery. By isolating and extending the ELD, we created a novel shuttle peptide, termed S237. While S237 achieved lower delivery of green fluorescent protein, it outperformed S10 at Cas9 RNP delivery to cultured human airway epithelial cells and to pig airway epithelia in vivo, possibly due to its lower net charge. In well-differentiated primary human airway epithelial cell cultures, S237 achieved a 4.6-fold increase in base editor RNP delivery, correcting up to 9.4% of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) R553X allele and restoring CFTR channel function close to non-CF levels. These findings deepen the understanding of peptide-mediated delivery and offer a translational approach for base editor RNP delivery for CF airway disease.

## Abstract

## Introduction

Since the demonstration of targeted genome cleavage in human cells by the CRISPR/Cas9 system (1), there has been a rapid expansion of gene editing toolkits, including the identification of novel CRISPR associated (Cas) nucleases (2–4) and the development of Cas-based DNA effectors (5–7), transposases/recombinases (8,9), base editors (10–12) and prime editors (13–15). These refined gene editing machineries offer great promise to address the fundamental causes of genetic diseases; however, translational advances require in vivo delivery systems enabling efficient entry of both the nuclease and its guide RNA (gRNA) to specific target cell types (16–18).

Epithelial cells lining the intrapulmonary airways present formidable barriers for delivery of gene editing machinery (19). Several delivery systems are being developed to improve in vivo delivery of Cas-based editing tools in the form of an encoding DNA or RNA, or as RNP complex including viruses (e.g. AAV, lentivirus and adenovirus), lipid nanoparticles, polymeric nanoparticles, extracellular vesicles, engineered capsids, virus-like particles and ultrasound (16–18). Even with this array of delivery systems, all with specific advantages and challenges, efficient and safe delivery methods still limit the use of CRISPR/Cas9 systems as treatments for airway diseases.

Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive genetic disease caused by mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator CFTR gene. Although ∼90% of CF patients could potentially benefit from CFTR modulator therapies, ∼10% of patients, including those with nonsense mutations, suffer from progressive lung disease and have limited treatment options (20,21). Adenine base editors (ABEs) were designed by fusing an evolved adenine deaminase enzyme to a nuclease-impaired Cas9 to specifically target point mutations by converting an A:T to G:C without creating DNA double-strand breaks (11,12). Using electroporation of ABE RNP, we and others characterized the functional correction of CFTR in human airway epithelial cells with CFTR nonsense mutations (22–24). These results demonstrate the potential of ABE RNP as a treatment for certain CFTR nonsense mutations.

Direct transduction of Cas or ABE RNP complexes into airway epithelial cells has the advantage of a rapid onset yet transient duration of exposure that should minimize undesired editing outcomes. We previously demonstrated the successful delivery of green fluorescent protein (GFP) and Cas12a and Cas9 RNPs to human airway epithelia in vitro using the S10 shuttle peptide (25). The S10 sequence was rationally designed by combining a cell penetrating peptide (CPP) with an amphiphilic endosomal leakage domain (ELD) to form a single synthetic peptide (25). This peptide-based delivery method also achieved a clinically relevant level of in vivo editing in the ROSAmT/mG mouse model (25).

Here, to understand and improve gene editing RNP delivery to airway epithelial cells, we investigated the contributions of the CPP and ELD to the S10 peptide delivery activity. Using circular dichroism (CD), we observed that S10 forms an alpha-helical structure in a membrane-mimicking trifluoroethanol (TFE) solution. By disrupting the alpha-helix formation of the S10 N-terminal domain using N-methyl amino acids, we observed that the ELD is critical for delivery activity; however, preventing the alpha-helix formation of the CPP-derived C-terminal domain did not affect delivery activity. We isolated the ELD, flanked it with poly glycine-serine (GS) stretches, and obtained a novel shuttle peptide, termed S237, that retained partial delivery activity despite the absence of the CPP-derived domain. In contrast to the parent S10 peptide whose activity was inhibited by the presence of Cas9 RNP, the S237 peptide maintained its delivery activity in presence of Cas9 RNP and enhanced delivery of Cas9 and ABE RNPs to well-differentiated human airway epithelial cells. We confirmed that the improved activity of S237 translates in vivo by delivering Cas9 RNP to pig airways. Finally, S237-dependent delivery of ABE8e-Cas9-NG RNP to primary cultures of human airway epithelia with CFTR R553X mutation restored CFTR function. These results advance our understanding of protein delivery facilitated by amphiphilic alpha-helical shuttle peptides and highlight the potential use of the novel S237 peptide for base editor RNP therapies towards CF and other lung diseases.

## Materials and methods

### Synthesized peptides and gRNAs

Shuttle peptides were synthesized by GL Biochem, Ltd (Shanghai, China). Lyophilized peptides were resuspended in PBS and diluted to a stock concentration of 250 μM for subsequent applications. gRNAs were purchased from IDT or Synthego. gRNA sequences are listed in Supplementary Table S1.

### Circular dichroism spectropolarimetry

Analyses of peptides in solution were performed with 1 mg/ml peptide in PBS, 25% TFE in PBS or 50% TFE in PBS. Spectra were recorded using 0.1 mm path length quartz cells. Ten scans were collected from 190 to 250 nm with a scanning speed of 100 nm/min using a Jasco J-815 spectropolarimeter (Easton, Maryland). Experiments were performed at 22°C. Each spectrum obtained in millidegrees (⊖) was converted in molar ellipticity (deg cm2 dmol−1) after subtraction of spectra of the buffer in absence of peptide. Data were reported as the mean residue ellipticity (26). Percentage of helix was calculated by dividing the mean residue ellipticity [φ]222obs by the reported [φ]222obs for a model helical decapeptide (26).

### Recombinant GFP-NLS, Cas9 and ABE8e-Cas9

Nuclear-targeted GFP (GFP-NLS) was expressed in bacteria (E. coli BL21DE3) and purified as previously described (27). Cas9 nuclease (catalog A034b-a-0500PMOL Feldan Therapeutics, Quebec, QC) was provided by Feldan Therapeutics.

The expression vector ABE8e-Cas9/pD881-SR was provided by Dr D. Liu (Broad Institute). The coding sequence includes a N-ter 6x-His tag and the protein expression is under the control of a rhamnose-inducible promoter. Point mutations were introduced to ABE8e-Cas9/pD881-SR to produce the NG PAM Cas9 variant (28). As reported previously (29), plasmids were transformed into E. coli BL21(DE3) pLysS strain (ThermoFisher). Protein expression was induced by adding 0.8% Rhamnose for 20–24 h before being harvested by centrifugation. The bacterial pellet was resuspended in 20 volumes (w/v) of lysis buffer (40 mM sodium phosphate, 200 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole, 10 mM MgCl2, 0.3% triton X-100, 10% glycerol; pH 7.5), 1 mM PMSF, 0.5 mg/ml lysozyme and 15 μg/ml DNAse I. The cell suspension was incubated at 4°C for 1 h with agitation. The cell lysate was then clarified by centrifugation at 12 500 g, at 10°C, for 40 min, following by a filtration step onto a 0.45 μM PES filter.

All purification steps were performed on an AKTApure 150 FPLC system (Cytiva). Firstly, the lysate was passed through a HisPrep FF 16/10 (Cytiva) previously equilibrated with the Hisprep buffer A (40 mM sodium phosphate, 500 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole, 10% glycerol; pH 7.5). After sample loading, the column was washed with 20 volumes of 4% heparin buffer B (40 mM sodium phosphate, 500 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole, 10% glycerol; pH 7.5), and the ABE8e-Cas9 containing fraction was eluted with 70% of buffer B. The eluted sample was diluted in 1 volume of heparin buffer A (40 mM sodium phosphate, 10% glycerol; pH7.2), and loaded onto 2 × 5 ml Hitrap heparin HP columns previously equilibrated with 20% buffer B (40 mM sodium phosphate, 1 M NaCl, 10% glycerol; pH 7.2). The ABE8e-Cas9 was eluted with a linear gradient from 20 to 100%B. Eluted fractions were pooled and concentrated using AMICON 100K (MilliporeSigma) before being loaded onto a Superdex 200 pg 26/600 in the storage buffer (25 mM HEPES, 350 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 1 mM DTT; pH 7.5). The peak corresponding to ABE8e-Cas9 protein dimers was concentrated on AMICON 100K to a final concentration of 40 μM.

### Cells and cell culture

CFF-16HBEge CFTR R553X cells were kindly provided by the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation (CFF) and cultured in aMEM media with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS). HeLa cells were purchased from ATCC (catalog# CCL-2) and cultured in DMEM with 10% FBS.

Primary airway epithelial cells isolated from human donor trachea or bronchi were grown at the air–liquid interface on collagen-coated Costar Transwell polycarbonate filters (#CLS3413, 0.33 cm2 surface area). Cultures were maintained in PneumaCult-ALI media (Stemcell Technologies, Catalog # 05001) and the following antibiotics: penicillin (50 U/ml), streptomycin (50 μg/ml), Amphotericin B (0.25 μg/ml) and gentamycin (50 μg/ml). The cultured cells were maintained at 37°C in 5% CO2. All epithelial cell cultures were well differentiated (>4 weeks maintained at air liquate interface (ALI); resistance > 1000 Ω × cm2).

### Delivery of GFP-NLS in the presence or absence of Cas RNP

For delivery in CFF-16HBEge CFTR R553X cells, 20000 cells were plated in each of the 96-well plate the day before the delivery. Different components were mixed in PBS with the final concentration of 10 μM recombinant GFP-NLS, 10 μM shuttle peptides with or without 2.5 μM Cas9/ABE8e-Cas9 and 2 μM gRNA. Delivery mix was applied to the cells 60 s before the removal of delivery mix and the wash of cells. The cells were trypsinized 1–4 h post-delivery and the percentage of the GFP positive cells was measured using flow cytometry. Relative cell viability was measured by the number of events monitored by flow cytometry after gating on cell size using forward scatter (FSC) parameter and cell granularity using side scatter (SSC) parameter. Relative viability percentage was calculated by comparing each delivery condition to the average of the mock condition. Example of the gating strategy is provided as Supplementary Figure S2A.

For the delivery in HeLa cells, 20 000 cells were plated in each of the 96-well plate the day before the delivery. Different components were mixed in RPMI plain media with the final concentration of 10 μM recombinant GFP-NLS and 7.5 μM shuttle peptide. Delivery mix was applied to the cells 5 min before the removal of the delivery mix and subsequent wash of the cells. The cells were trypsinized 1–4 h post-delivery and GFP positive cells were visualized by epifluorescent microscopy and quantified by flow cytometry with similar gating strategy as for CFF-16HBEge cells.

### Delivery of CRISPR nucleases and adenine base editors

Delivery of Cas RNP to cells in vitro was performed as described previously (29). Briefly, Cas9 or ABE8e-Cas9 nucleases were mixed with gRNA and diluted to a final concentration of 2.5 μM of nuclease and 2 μM of gRNA in PBS. The RNP was then combined with 40 μM of shuttle peptides for delivery to HBE-ALI culture for 3 h. The delivery mix was removed after the respective delivery time. For ABE8e-Cas9 RNP delivery in human bronchial epithelia in culture at an air liquid interface (HBE-ALI), the delivery was performed three times, 48–72 h apart each. Guide RNA sequences are listed in Supplementary Table S1.

### Delivery of DRI-NLS-Cy5 and Cas9 RNP to pig airways

All procedures used in live animals conformed to the requirements of the Animal Welfare Act, and protocols were reviewed and approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at the University of Missouri. Transgenic GFP pigs between 4 and 5 weeks old were randomly assigned to the treatments. One pig was used to evaluate the biodistribution of the fluorescent protein cargo DRI-NLS-Cy5 (10 μM) administered to the porpoise lobe together with the shuttle peptide S237 (40 μM). Other pigs were used to examine the editing of the GFP locus in the airway epithelial cells of the porpoise lobe after administration of the Cas9 RNP (Cas9 2.5 μM/gRNA 2 μM targeting GFP locus) and two shuttle peptides, 40 μM S10 (n = 2) and 40 μM S237 (n = 2). One control animal received a sterile DPBS in the same manner as the experimental ones.

Animals were anesthetized and sedated with intra-muscular injection of Ketamine and Xylazine (Ketamine: 20 mg/kg; Xylazine: 2 mg/kg dose) and monitored during the period of anesthesia and until fully recovered. Anesthetized animals were positioned on their right side, airway access was assured with a laryngeal mask airway (LMA) and the instillation into the porpoise lobe was performed using the Ambu aScope 4 Broncho Slim 3.8/1.2 under visual guidance with the Ambu aView Monitor (both Ambu Inc, Columbia, MD, Ref# 476001000 and Ref # 405001000, resp.). Two ml of the instillation solution were instilled into each of the two sub-lobar airways of the porpoise lobe, followed by 2 ml of ambient air in each sub-lobar region to complete the instillation and clear the materials left in the bronchoscope. In instances where the sub-lobar airway diameter did not allow for individual instillation, the entire volume of the instillation solution (4 ml) was instilled into the main lobar airway of the porpoise lobe, followed by 4 ml of ambient air. After instillation, the animals were positioned on their right side and monitored closely during the post-administration period. For the pig instilled with the fluorescent cargo (DRI-NLS-Cy5), the tissues were collected 1-h post-instillation. For pigs instilled with Cas9 RNP, the instillation was repeated the next day and tissues were harvested 6 days after the last instillation.

Following euthanasia (Euthasol®), the chest cavity was opened, and the large vessels were cut at the level of the diaphragm. The animal instilled with the fluorescent cargo DRI-NLS-Cy5 were processed as follows. With the lungs in situ, the trachea was fitted with PE tubing and the lungs were lavaged once with PBS by gravity perfusion to remove any remaining instillation solution. Next, the lungs were inflated with 4% paraformaldehyde (PF) fixative under the gravity of a 30 cm water column. The trachea was tied off, the lungs were dissected from the chest cavity, placed in a container with 4% PF, and fixed at 4°C for a minimum of 48 h. The lungs were processed in 15% and 30% sucrose gradient, and the porpoise lobe was dissected into blocks that were embedded in OCT, and cryosectioned for microscopy.

For the gene-edited animals, following euthanasia, the lung lobes were removed en bloc with the heart, and each lobe was dissected in order to access the main lobar airway and collect the airway epithelial brushings. Trachea, mainstem bronchi, each lobar airway, and each of the two sub-lobar airways of the porpoise lobe were brushed using individual sterile cytological brushes by gently rotating the brushes several times (Ref 25-2199, Puritan Medical Products Company LLC, Guilford, ME; or ConMed Disposable Bronchial Cytology Brush, ConMed Corporation, Utica, NY). Brushes were then placed into 1.5 ml of PBS in snap cap tubes and transported on ice to the processing laboratory. The lobes were placed into the 4% PF fixative. The epithelia were dissociated from the brushes by mechanically agitating and swirling the brushes and vortexing. The brushings were centrifuged at 5000 g and the pellets were reconstituted in 20 μl QuickExtract. An aliquot of the genomic DNA (gDNA) was used for the next generation sequencing.

### Delivery of adenine base editor to mouse airways

To investigate the ability of ABE8e to repair a premature termination codon (PTC) and restore protein function in vivo, we used the GER10 mice—R26-GFP_KI-ABE (Adenine Base Editor) reporter knock-in mice (C57BL/6N-Gt(ROSA)26Sorem3(CAG-Venus*)Rkuhn/MurrMmjax, MMRRC Strain #069724-JAX (jax.org/strain/034450)). These mice express a CAG promoter controlling expression of a non-functional mVenus reporter gene disrupted by a premature termination codon (Q81X) that can be reverted using an ABE to activate mVenus expression. Homozygous mice (male and female) between 6 and12 weeks of age were lightly anesthetized and instilled intranasally with 50 μl of one of the following: (i) a combination of S237 peptide (40 μM) and RNP (ABE8e-Cas9-NGG 2.5 μM, sgRNA 2 μM), (ii) RNP alone or (iii) RPMI (control) twice on two consecutive days. The mice were euthanized 7–9 days after the last instillation, and the vasculature was perfused via the heart with 15 ml cold PBS, followed by 15 ml of 4% PF. The lungs with tracheas were removed, fixed in 4% PF, processed in 30% sucrose, and shipped to the processing laboratory.

### Lung microscopy

Lung tissues were embedded in OCT and stored at −80°C prior to processing for microscopy. Cryosections (10 μm) were adhered to CryoJane adhesive coated slides (Ref 3 P 39475208 CFSA 1X Leica Microsystems), rehydrated in PBS, and stained with acetylated-α-tubulin antibody to stain ciliated cells, and/or Muc5ac antibody to stain mucus producing secretory cells as previously described (28). Briefly, the sections were permeabilized and blocked with 10% animal serum in which the secondary antibodies were raised. Primary antibodies at 1:50–1:100 dilution were incubated overnight at 4°C, and secondary antibodies at 1:500–1:1000 dilution were incubated for 60–120 min at room temperature. The coverslips were mounted with Vectashield with DAPI and slides were imaged by an automated slide scanner (PANNORAMIC MIDI II, 3DHistech Ltd) or a confocal microscope with a 40× objective and oil correction (Zeiss LSM 710). Where applicable, images of 0.5 μm z-sections were collected using the Zen software (Zeiss) and ImageJ/FIJI (ImageJ, NIH) was used to make the maximum intensity projections of between 1 and 10 μm tissue thickness. Minimal adjustments of the intensity/contrast were used to optimize the images on a computer screen. Localization of DRI-NLS-Cy5 (indicating a successful delivery in the pig) or GFP (indicating an editing in GER10 mice) in the airway epithelial cell subsets was investigated. In the GER10 mice lungs, the ciliated cells were identified by AcTub staining, and the secretory cells were identified based on their typical morphology including the presence of the pre-formed secretory granules demonstrating as circular voids in the GFP-emitting cytoplasm of edited cells and the lack of AcTub staining. The following staining antibodies were used: Muc5ac (MUC5AC, 45M1, Invitrogen, Ref # MA5-12178), and anti-acetylated tubulin (AcTub, Sigma-Aldrich, Ref # T6793 and Signaling Technology, Ref #5335). Species matched secondary antibodies were conjugated with AF546 and AF647.

### Next-generation sequencing and analysis

Genomic DNA was isolated using QuickExtract (catalog #QE09050, Lucigen, Middleton, WI) according to the manufacturer's protocol. The target locus was PCR amplified (KAPA DNA polymerase, Roche, Basel, Switzerland) using primers with the appropriate Illumina forward and reverse adaptors. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table S1. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) using the Illumina MiSeq instrument was performed as previously reported (29). Indel frequencies were assessed using the software package CRISPResso2 (30). Indels were defined as detectable if there was a significant difference (Student's two-tailed t-test, P < 0.05) between indel formation in the treated sample and untreated control. For gene editing efficiency in pig airway samples, the editing percentage in delivered samples was calculated by subtracting the sequencing background in the mock sample.

To report the base editing efficiency obtained in primary airway epithelia isolated from donor that was compound heterozygous for CFTR R553X/L671X mutations, the percent allelic editing efficiencies were adjusted from the high throughput sequencing data using the formula (% base edited-50)/50 × 100 (24)

### LDH assay

The LDH assay was performed as described previously (25). Primary airway epithelial cell cultures from non-CF human donors were incubated with the S10 or S237 peptide alone or co-incubated with ABE RNP (2.5μM ABE8e-Cas9-NG/2μM sgRNA targeting CFTR R553X) in a 50 μl volume for 15 min. The apical surface was washed, and the basolateral media collected at the indicated time points post-incubation. CyQUANT™ LDH Cytotoxicity Assay kit (C20300, ThermoFisher) was used to measure the LDH levels in the apical surface washes and basolateral media. The percentage of toxicity and viability were calculated based on LDH levels. Data were normalized to cells treated with media containing 1% Triton X-100 (positive control) on the apical surface for 45 min at 37°C.

### Electrophysiology

Eight days after the first delivery, well-differentiated airway epithelial cultures were mounted in the Ussing chambers and examined for changes in short circuit current in response to stimuli as previously reported (31). Airway epithelial cell cultures were pre-stimulated overnight with forskolin (10 μM; Cayman Chemical, Ann Arbor, MI) and 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine (IBMX) (100 μM; Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO) (F&I). Cell cultures were mounted in the Ussing chambers, bathed in symmetrical Ringer's solution (135 mM NaCl, 5 mM HEPES, 0.6 mM KH2PO4, 2.4 mM K2HPO4, 1.2 mM MgCl2, 1.2 mM CaCl2, 5 mM Dextrose), transepithelial voltage (Vt) was maintained at 0, and baseline currents were established. CFTR current was measured using the following protocol: amiloride (100 μM), 4,4′-dilsothiocyano-2,2′-stilbenedifulonic acid (DIDS) (100 μM; both Sigma Aldrich, St Louis, MO), F&I, followed by the CFTR channel inhibitor GlyH-101 (GlyH).

### Statistical analysis

Student's two-tailed t-test, or one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey's multiple comparison test (as indicated in the figure legends) were used to analyze differences between groups’ means. Results are expressed as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). P values ≤0.05 were considered significant.

## Results

### Helical structure of N-terminal ELD is critical for S10 function

CPPs are short peptides generally carrying a net positive charge and typically covalently fused with cargos to mediate their internalization into cells (32). However, endosomal sequestration following CPP-mediated delivery often limits cytosolic availability of the cargo (33). To avoid the endosomal entrapment characteristic of CPP-mediated delivery, we previously designed the S10 shuttle peptide by fusing an ELD with a CPP domain connected by a poly-glycine linker (Figure 1A) (25,27,34). In contrast to standard strategies using CPPs, the S10 peptide is not covalently linked to the cargo, but is co-incubated with a cargo, enabling its cytoplasmic delivery without endosomal entrapment after a brief incubation with cells (25,27).

*Figure 1.: Peptide S10 sequence and structure. (A) Amino acid sequence and schematic structure of S10 peptide. ELD-derived, linker and CPP-derived domains are shown. Cationic residues are highlighted in blue, highly hydrophobic residues in gray, polar residues in orange, weekly hydrophobic residues in yellow. Predicted secondary structure by software PyMol is illustrated. (B) Circular dichroism spectroscopy analysis of S10 in PBS solution containing 0%, 25% or 50% TFE. Alpha-helix structures are characterized by a maximal wavelength at 190 nm, and a minimal at 208 nm as observed for S10 in solutions containing 25 or 50% TFE. Disordered structures are characterized by a minimal wavelength of 195 nm and maximal at 212 nm as observed for S10 in PBS solution (no TFE). (C) Percentage of alpha-helix structure formed by S10 peptide in PBS solution containing 0%, 25% or 50% TFE. Column heights represent means and error bars represent SD. n = 2 per group.*

The S10 N-terminal ELD sequence is rich in highly hydrophobic and cationic residues designed to form an amphiphilic alpha-helix with cationic residues displayed on one side and hydrophobic residues oriented on the opposite side of the peptide (Figure 1A), features devised to interact and destabilize the lipid membrane and facilitate endosomal escape. The C-terminal domain is characterized by the presence of cationic amino acids and was derived from CPPs (35). It has been suggested that the helical structure of CPPs contributes to their ability to pass through cell membranes and enable effective delivery (36,37). Using circular dichroism (CD) spectra, we confirmed that S10 peptide is mostly unstructured in an aqueous solution (no TFE), featuring a minimal wavelength at 195 nm and a close to zero ellipticity above 210 nm. In contrast, S10 adopts an alpha-helical structure in membrane-mimicking TFE solutions of 25% and 50% with a positive maximum around 193 nm and negative minima at 208 nm and 222 nm (Figure 1B). The graphical representation of the percentage of alpha-helix is displayed in Figure 1C (38).

To further understand the functional contribution of the S10 alpha-helix structure observed by CD, we replaced two amino acids within the N- or C-terminal domains of S10 with N-methyl (Nme) amino acids (Figure 2A). The methyl group of Nme amino acids prevents the formation of hydrogen bonds required to stabilize the alpha-helix structure (39). We observed that the inclusion of Nme amino acids in the N-terminal ELD-derived domain (S10-methyl-N2) decreased the alpha-helix formation previously observed in TFE solution (Figure 2B, C). In contract, the S10 alpha-helix profile was retained in the TFE solution when Nme amino acids was incorporated in the C-terminal CPP-derived domain (S10-methyl-C2) (Figure 2D, E). These results suggest that the N-terminal domain is the main contributor to the alpha-helix conformation of S10 measured by CD.

*Figure 2.: N-Methyl amino acids incorporated in S10 N-terminal sequence decrease alpha-helix level and delivery activity. (A) Sequence of S10 peptide and N-methyl peptides S10-methyl-N2/C2. N-terminal ELD-derived domain is colored in green, linker in black, and C-terminal CPP-derived domain in blue. (B) Circular dichroism spectroscopy analysis of S10-methyl-N2 peptide in the presence of 0, 25, and 50% TFE. (C) Percentage of alpha-helix structure of S10-methyl-N2 peptide in the presence of 0, 25 and 50% TFE. (D) Circular dichroism spectroscopy analysis of S10-methyl-C2 peptide in the presence of 0, 25 and 50% TFE. (E) Percentage of alpha-helix structure of S10-methyl-C2 peptide in the presence of 0, 25 and 50% TFE. (F) Epifluorescence microscopy images of HeLa cells after delivery of 10 μM GFP-NLS using 7.5μM of respective shuttle peptides. (G) Percentage of GFP positive cells after delivery of 10μM GFP-NLS with 7.5 μM of peptides to HeLa cells, as measured by flow cytometry. Column heights represent means and error bars represent SEM, n = 4 replicates per group.*

To investigate the contributions of the alpha-helical structure to protein delivery activity, we co-incubated S10 or either Nme containing peptides (S10-methyl-N2/C2) with recombinant GFP tagged with a nuclear localization signal (GFP-NLS) on HeLa cells. Successful delivery of GFP-NLS to the cytoplasm without endosomal entrapment will lead to nuclear import of GFP-NLS. We observed the nuclear GFP signal by epifluorescence microscopy (Figure 2F) and quantified protein delivery activity by measuring the percentage of GFP positive cells using flow cytometry (Figure 2G). In addition to inhibiting the alpha-helix formation of S10 (Figure 2B, C), the incorporation of Nme amino acids into the N terminal ELD markedly reduced the delivery activity (Figure 2F, G). In contrast, the introduction of Nme amino acids within the C-terminal CPP-derived domain did not significantly alter alpha-helix formation (Figure 2D, E) or the S10 delivery properties (Figure 2F, G). These results suggest that the alpha-helical structure of the S10 ELD-derived N-terminal sequence is a critical functional domain responsible for its delivery properties.

### N-terminal ELD-derived domain of S10 alone retains delivery activity but requires flanking amino acids

To further dissect the functional contributions of the N- and C-terminal domains, we designed peptides containing only the S10 N-terminal ELD-derived (S10-Nter) or C-terminal CPP-derived (S10-Cter) domains (Figure 3A). We measured the protein delivery activity of the S10, S10-Nter and S10-Cter peptides by delivering recombinant GFP-NLS to HeLa cells as described above. As previously demonstrated (27), the CPP or ELD alone, without modifications or fusion with a protein cargo, exhibited no cell delivery properties after a 5-minute incubation with cells (Figure 3B).

In a previous study we observed that adding amino acid stretches to the N- or C-terminal ends of an ELD-CPP peptide increased its protein delivery properties (27). As the alpha-helix structure of the ELD is essential for delivery, we hypothesized that lengthening the ends of the peptide might further extend the alpha-helix structure. To test the effects of additional amino acid extensions on delivery activity, we synthetized the S10 N- and C-terminal domains with added GS stretches on both ends to form the S10-Nter-GS and S10-Cter-GS peptides (Figure 3A). Figure 3B presents the GFP-NLS delivery properties of S10-Nter-GS and S10-Cter-GS peptides. While the S10-Cter peptide derived from CPP failed to confer delivery activity with or without added poly GS extensions, the N-terminal module derived from ELD exhibited partial delivery capacity only with the poly GS sequences. We designated this new S10-Nter-GS peptide ‘S237’ based on its numerical ranking in our peptide bank.

### S237 improves Cas9 RNP delivery in vitro

Previously, we observed that the delivery activity of S10 peptide for protein cargoes was inhibited by the presence of Cas9 crRNA and tracrRNA, and partially inhibited by Cas9 RNP, possibly due to cationic/anionic interactions which diminished S10 availability to bind and destabilize cell membranes (25). S237 has a reduced cationic charge density (+6) compared to S10 (+10) due to the absence of the CPP (Figure 3A). Therefore, we hypothesized that the S237 delivery activity would be less susceptible to Cas9 RNP inhibition, despite having approximately one third of the S10 delivery activity for GFP-NLS (Figure 3B). As reported (29), we assessed the inhibitory effects of Cas9 RNP on S10 and S237 by measuring the delivery efficiency of the GFP-NLS to the CF airway epithelial cell line CFF-16HBEge in the presence or absence of Cas9 RNP. As observed previously, we noted that S10 GFP-NLS delivery efficiency was inhibited in the presence of Cas9-RNP (29). Consistent with our hypothesis, the S237, despite providing an overall lower activity than S10, fully maintained its GFP-NLS delivery capacity in the presence of Cas9 RNP, demonstrating a resistance to the inhibitory effects of Cas9 RNP (Figure 3C, Supplementary Figure S2A). Of note, the cell viability was similar between S10 and S237 as measured by flow cytometry (Supplementary Figure S2B).

To evaluate whether the observed resistance of S237 to the inhibition by Cas9 RNP would translate into improved Cas9 RNP delivery, we applied S10 and S237 to well-differentiated primary human bronchial epithelial cells at ALI with Cas9 RNP targeting the CFTR locus as reported previously (29). We observed a significantly higher gene editing using S237 compared to the S10 peptide, reaching up to ∼14% editing (Figure 3D). As reported for S10 (25), we observed no cell toxicity on HBE-ALI culture incubated with effective doses of S10 or S237 (Supplementary Figure S3).

### S237 improves Cas9 RNP delivery to porcine airway epithelia in vivo

To confirm that the improved delivery properties of S237 would translate in vivo, we compared the delivery of Cas9 RNP using S10 and S237 in neonatal pigs. The lungs of this large animal model share many anatomical, histological, biochemical and physiologic features with human lungs (40,41). For this experiment we selected transgenic pigs expressing eGFP (42), and used Cas9 RNP targeting the GFP locus. We focused our analysis on a single lung lobe and delivered the materials into the porpoise lobe (right upper lobe equivalent) with a bronchoscope as described in Methods. We first examined the in vivo delivery using a Cy5-labeled peptide cargo composed of a nuclear localization signal (NLS) sequence made of D-amino acids, termed DRI-NLS-Cy5. Using a co-delivery with S237 peptide and collection of the lung tissue after 1 h post-delivery, we observed a successful intracellular delivery of the DRI-NLS-Cy5 peptide cargo to the nucleus without endosomal entrapment (29,43). As shown in Figure 4A–C, the S237 peptide facilitated delivery of the DRI-Cy5-NLS cargo to the ciliated and secretory cells of the airways, and was similar to that of S10 (25,29). Having validated this administration approach, we next delivered the Cas9 RNP targeting the eGFP locus of transgenic pig using S10 or S237. The editing was quantified by NGS as the heterogeneity of the eGFP expression in the airway cells observed by fluorescence microscopy precluded quantification. One-week post-administration, epithelial cells from the porpoise lobe two main segmental airways were collected using cytology brushes, gDNA was isolated and subjected to NGS. As shown in Figure 4D, the editing efficiency (% indels) was greater when the Cas9 nuclease was delivered using S237, achieving up to ∼10% editing. These results demonstrate that in vitro findings of superior delivery activity with the S237 peptide translate into improved delivery and gene editing in vivo.

### Functional correction of the CFTR R553X mutation in well-differentiated primary human CF airway epithelia

Base editors have therapeutic potential to precisely correct single base point mutations without introducing DNA double-strand breaks, a significant advantage over conventional Cas9 nuclease editing. ABE8e-Cas9 is an evolved adenine base editor with an improved A > G editing efficiency (44). We hypothesized that sufficient delivery of ABE8e-Cas9 RNP targeting a disease-causing point mutation could achieve therapeutically relevant correction of phenotype. As ABE8e-Cas9 uses the RNA-guided activity of a catalytically impaired Cas9 and an identical gRNA strategy to that of the Cas9 nuclease, we speculated that S237 could resist the inhibition by the RNP and show higher base editing efficiency than S10, as observed for Cas9 RNP (Figure 3D). As observed with Cas9 RNP, we observed a relative higher resistance of S237 to inhibition by ABE8e-Cas9 compared to S10 (Figure 5A) and a significantly increased A > G conversion using S237 in primary HBE-ALI culture (Figure 5B). Interestingly, we noticed overall higher % base editing post ABE8e-Cas9 delivery compared to % INDEL after the delivery of Cas9 RNP using the same guide RNA (Supplementary Figure S4). This is potentially due to the higher activity of the evolved deoxyadenosine deaminase contained in ABE8e-Cas9 over the nuclease activity of the Cas9 enzyme.

We next demonstrated the potential of S237-mediated base editor delivery to correct a premature termination codon mutation and restore a protein expression in respiratory epithelia in vivo. The GER10 mouse model expresses a non-functional mVenus protein disrupted by an engineered stop codon (jax.org/strain/034450). Instillation of S237 and ABE8e-Cas9 RNP targeting the stop codon led to restoration of mVenus protein expression visualized as green fluorescent signal in the surface epithelial cells of both the large and small airways throughout the lungs. Importantly, mVenus-evidenced editing and expression occurred in both the secretory (predominantly) and ciliated airway epithelial cell subtypes (Supplementary Figure S6). We note that secretory cells are the most abundant cell type expressing CFTR in the in the respiratory tract (45). These results demonstrate that the S237 shuttle peptide is an effective and efficient delivery agent targeting several airway surface epithelial cell types with base editor RNPs for correction of nonsense mutations and restoration of a protein function.

To evaluate the base editor delivery in a pulmonary disease model, we tested the correction of the nonsense R553X CFTR mutation using primary HBE cells cultured at the air-liquid interface, a robust and widely used model for drug discovery in cystic fibrosis research. The R553X CFTR mutation features a C > T substitution in exon 11, introducing a premature stop-codon and a resultant truncated non-functional CFTR protein that is nonresponsive to CFTR modulator therapies (46,47). The PAM permissive ABE8e-Cas9-NG was purified and used as RNP to enable the targeting of the R553X mutation in primary human CF airway epithelial cells cultured at the ALI after differentiation (29) (Figure 5C). The ABE8e-Cas9-NG RNP was applied to the apical surface of epithelia with S10 or S237 peptide. One week post-delivery, CFTR-dependent Cl− transport was studied in Ussing chambers and then cells were harvested to determine the editing efficiency by high throughput sequencing. As shown in Figure 5D, we observed an editing efficiency of 9.39% using S237 while S10 reached 2.04%, representing a 4.6-fold improvement. Furthermore, while ABE RNP delivery with S10 partially restored CFTR-dependent anion transport, the level of editing achieved by S237 delivery improved CFTR-dependent anion transport to levels similar to non-CF cells (Figure 5E, F).

## Discussion

Following a decade of development, CRISPR-based toolkits have made remarkable progress toward human therapies. Despite tremendous clinical advances ex vivo (48), targeting somatic cells in vivo beyond the eye (49) and liver (50) remains challenging (16,17). Using electroporation, we recently demonstrated that ABE RNP offers a potential therapy for a subset of CF patients by restoring CFTR function in cells with premature stop codon mutations (R553X and W1282X) and a splice-site mutation (3849 + 10 kb C > T) with minimal bystander edits or indels (24). Using electroporation, we recently showed that an enhanced prime editing system in an RNA format could restore function of the CFTR F508del mutation (15). However, translational delivery strategies for base and prime editing applications in patient-derived airway epithelial cells and the airways in vivo are lacking.

Airway epithelial cells cultured at an air-liquid interface recapitulate key features of the airway epithelial barrier and cellular composition, forming a pseudostratified layer with basal, secretory, and ciliated cells similar to human airways (51). Direct delivery to the apical surface of primary HBE cells cultured at the air-liquid interface from people with cystic fibrosis represents a gold standard model of the field. Here we improved Cas9 and ABE RNP delivery using the novel S237 peptide, demonstrated in vivo editing by delivering Cas9 RNP to porcine airway epithelia, and achieved therapeutically relevant base editing and correction of the CFTR R553X mutation in CF patient-derived primary airway epithelial cells. This delivery strategy offers promise for potential therapeutic applications and overcomes some of the limitations of viral vector technologies.

S10 peptide was originally designed to contain a CPP domain to mediate cell membrane penetration and an ELD to assist endosomal escape (27). Studying the secondary structure of S10, we observed that the incorporation of Nme amino acids in the ELD-derived N-terminal domain abrogated both the alpha-helix structure observed in CD (Figure 2B, C) and the GFP delivery activity (Figure 2F, G), indicating the critical contribution of the ELD to the S10 delivery activity. In contrast, Nme amino acids inserted in the C-terminal CPP domain of S10 did not decrease alpha-helix formation (Figure 2D, E) and the delivery activity was retained (Figure 2F, G). These results suggest that the alpha-helical structure of S10 observed by CD is mainly due to the alpha-helix formation by the N-terminal domain. This also suggests that the S10 C-terminal domain remains mostly unstructured even in TFE, consistent with our observation (Supplementary Figure S1C, D). In agreement with our results, it was previously reported that CPP such as TAT and PTD4 do not form a strong alpha-helix structure (52).

As it was counterintuitive to our ELD-CPP design strategy, we were surprised to find that a peptide containing the ELD N-terminal domain while lacking the CPP domain could mediate protein delivery on its own. As measured in Figure 3B, the addition of GS extensions to both ends of the ELD domain was required to enable GFP delivery. In alpha helical peptides, the terminal turns of an alpha-helix contain three amide hydrogens (N-terminal) and three carbonyl groups (C-terminal) that lack subsequent amino acids to form backbone hydrogen bonds to stabilize the alpha-helix (53). Therefore, the GS extensions may provide these amino acids to form proper backbone hydrogen bonds, allowing partial alpha-helix formation at the S237 terminus when compared to S10-Nter alone (Figure 3A, and Supplementary Figure S1A, B). It is suggested that helix length contributes to the peptide's ability to destabilize cell membranes (54) and this may explain the inability of S10-Nter to deliver GFP without GS extensions, as the ELD cannot fully form the alpha-helix structure. In the S10 peptide, it is possible that the unstructured C-terminal domain combined with the flexible linker can bend to reach and stabilize the N-terminal alpha-helix of the ELD-derived domain as seen in miniproteins (55). This may explain why S10 delivers protein despite the absence of an extension at its N-terminal end.

We observed that S10 GFP delivery activity (60%) was higher than that achieved by S237 (S10-Nter-GS) (24%) (Figure 3B). Because S237 lacks a CPP, this suggests that the CPP-derived domain is not required but plays a synergistic role in protein delivery, boosting the ELD-delivery efficiency. One possible role of the CPP is to promote a stronger interaction with cells through its cationic charges that could bind to anionic molecules such as cell surface-expressed heparan sulfate glycosaminoglycans (56). As the S237 peptide lacks the CPP domain, we concluded that the ELD amphiphilic alpha-helix domain, co-incubated with GFP, Cas9, and ABE RNPs, is sufficient to facilitate cargo delivery. While the precise mechanism of action of S237 remains to be elucidated, it is possible that the cationic side of the ELD-derived helix (Figure 1A) could partially play the role of a CPP. It is also possible that the hydrophobic residues of S237 can directly interact with the lipids of the cell membrane but not as efficiently as when the CPP is present. In either case, when accumulated in sufficient concentration within the cell membrane, the ELD domain with the cargo at proximity will be internalized by cells through endocytic pathways (27). We speculate that the ELD present in S10 and S237 will destabilize the cell membrane lipids during the early endosomal process, resulting in a rapid release of the internalized cargo into the cell cytoplasm.

Unexpectedly and in contrast to GFP delivery, S237 demonstrated enhanced delivery of Cas9/ABE8e RNP to cultured human airway epithelia and in porcine airways in vivo. This represents an important advancement for gene editor delivery with shuttle peptides and provides a translational method for the application of base editor RNP for pulmonary diseases. S237 delivery activity was less inhibited by the presence of Cas9 or ABE8e RNP compared to S10. This may be explained by the overall lower cationic charge density of S237 (+6) when compared to S10 (+10), limiting interactions with the negatively charged phosphate backbone of the gRNA.

The airways of pigs share many similarities with human airways. We established a bronchoscopic administration method to deliver Cas9 RNP with S10 or S237 into the pig porpoise lobe (right upper lobe equivalent). By sequencing gDNA extracted from the epithelial cell brushings from the upper and lower segmental airways of the porpoise lobe, we confirmed that the superior delivery of Cas9 RNP by S237 observed in human airway cell models could be translated in vivo. Despite having only two animals per group, the mean INDEL percentage measured in airway epithelial cells from the lower lobe was 8.35% using S237 compared to 4.30% editing for S10. For the upper lobe, editing with S237 attained up to 10.8% editing. As the materials were delivered at the bifurcation of the lower and upper segmental airways, it is possible that less material reached the upper lobe in one animal, explaining the lower editing observed in this area (Figure 4D). Using the same administration method, we delivered a DRI-NLS-Cy5 peptide and determined that S237 enables delivery mainly to secretory and ciliated cells, similar to S10 (Figure 4B, C) (25,29,43). This may suggest that the cell types receiving the cargo is driven by the ELD domain shared by S237 and S10 and that the presence of a CPP domain in S10 does not influence the delivery profile of the peptide.

Building on the superior Cas9 RNP delivery activity of S237 observed on HBE-ALI and in pig airway in vivo, we compared S10 and S237 mediated-delivery of ABE8e-Cas9-NG RNP targeting CFTR R553X using primary human airway epithelial cells (R553X/L671X) cultured at the ALI. We confirmed that S237 achieved an allelic editing efficiency of the CFTR R553X mutation reaching 9.39% while S10 achieved an ∼2% editing efficiency (Figure 5D). ABE8e-Cas9 RNP delivered by S237 conferred functional restoration of CFTR activity in primary HBE ALI cultures, similar to the non-CF epithelia used as controls. Several studies suggest that correction of 10–50% of epithelial cells, either by mixing non-CF and CF cells or by analyzing different genotypes, is sufficient to confer normal CFTR activity (57–59). It has been recognized that CFTR expression is highly variable among different cell types within the surface airway epithelium. Secretory cells dominate CFTR expression in human airway epithelia (45). Ionocytes are rare but express the highest CFTR transcript levels (45,60,61). Ionocytes were recently demonstrated to play a role in airway surface liquid absorption (62,63). Our previous studies showed that S10-delivered GFP or Cy5 positive cells colocalize with markers of ciliated, non-ciliated, and goblet cells in human and mouse (25) and rhesus airway epithelia (29). In this study, we confirmed that S237 enables delivery of a DRI-NLS-Cy5 peptide to similar cell types in pig airway epithelia in vivo. We also confirmed that ABE RNP delivery by S237 can restore protein function in airway epithelia by correcting an engineered stop codon in the mVenus gene of the GER10 mouse model (Supplementary Figure S5 and S6). It is interesting that despite the relatively lower base editing efficiency achieved at the CFTR R553X locus by S237 delivery of ABE when compared to electroporation (24), the restoration of CFTR function was similar. We hypothesized that this could be explained by the shuttle peptide being more effective in its delivery of ABE to the secretory cells (Supplementary Figure S6), which are the predominant airway cell type expressing CFTR and contributing to the CFTR-mediated chloride secretion in the lungs (45).

This study has limitations. Measuring short circuit current responses is a very sensitive, specific, and informative endpoint to report successful restoration of CFTR function. However, this method does not provide direct measurement of CFTR protein abundance at the cell surface that links the base editing efficiency with ion channel activity measured in the Ussing chamber. Our attempts to quantify CFTR protein abundance in patient-derived primary airway epithelial cells that demonstrated 9.4% correction by NGS were unsuccessful. However, CFTR is a very low-abundance membrane protein in both human lung samples and in well differentiated primary cultures, and its quantification remains a technical challenge (64). A standardized, sensitive, reliable, and reproducible methodology for CFTR quantification in human airway tissues and primary airway cells is still an unmet need in the CF field and could potentially address this limitation of our study.

In conclusion, this study advances our understanding of key features required in amphiphilic alpha-helical shuttle peptides for delivery of cargoes such as Cas9 and ABE RNPs. The S237 peptide enables therapeutically relevant base editing of the R553X CFTR gene in primary well-differentiated patient-derived airway cells, providing a strategy for clinical optimization.
